summaries.example: Imagine a sentence pattern: “If ___ is sunny, then ___ is warm.” A rule might say that both blanks must use the same place name. Filling both blanks with “the park” gives: “If the park is sunny, then the park is warm.” The pattern is not itself a complete sentence; it is a recipe for making sentences.
summaries.summary: A schema is a pattern made from words or symbols, blanks, and instructions for using the blanks. Following the instructions creates particular expressions called instances. For example, the pattern “A; if A then B; therefore B” can become many arguments when A and B are replaced by sentences. Schemas help logicians describe rules of reasoning and axioms, help mathematicians express endlessly many principles such as induction, and help explain how a definition of truth should work. The entry also asks what a schema really is. Its written pattern is a string of symbols, while its filling instructions are a different, more abstract part. Philosophers may focus on the pattern, the rules, or the collection of results it produces, but these are not exactly the same thing. Schemas have a long history, with important examples connected to Aristotle and modern logicians such as Tarski.
key_ideas: A schema is like a carefully controlled recipe for making many expressions.
The finished expressions are called instances of the schema.
Schemas can describe sentence patterns, argument patterns, logic rules, and mathematical rules.
A schema is not usually true or false by itself, because it is a pattern rather than a complete sentence.
The same-looking pattern can work differently when its filling rules or language change.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schemas let people describe many related cases without writing every case separately. This is useful when there may be infinitely many cases. Learning about schemas also teaches an important lesson: a symbol that looks like a variable may instead be a blank in a recipe. Keeping those ideas apart helps us understand logic and mathematics more carefully.

important_terms.definition: A pattern with blanks and rules for filling them in. It can produce many complete sentences, arguments, or formulas.
A completed expression made by filling the blanks in a schema according to its rules.
A blank or dummy mark in a pattern that stands for something to be put there later.
A special rule explaining what may go into each placeholder and sometimes what the symbols mean.

questions_to_think_about: How is a pattern different from one finished example?
Why might a rule require two blanks to be filled with the same sentence?
Can you make a pattern that produces several different valid arguments?
Why would mathematicians want one rule that describes many separate statements?

summaries.example: Consider the argument pattern: A; if A, then B; therefore B. With A = “The sample is made of copper” and B = “The sample conducts electricity,” the result is an argument-text. The letters A and B are placeholders in the schema, not variables ranging over physical objects. A side condition requires each repeated letter to receive the same sentence, so changing only one occurrence would not produce a permitted instance.
summaries.summary: A schema is a linguistic or formal pattern plus rules that determine how it yields potentially many instances. The pattern may contain words, symbols, and placeholders; the side condition says what language the instances use and how substitutions must be made. This explains why a schema is not simply an incomplete sentence. An object-language variable ranges over objects in a domain, while a schema placeholder is a metalanguage device for inserting expressions. Schemas may generate sentences, smaller expressions, or argument-texts. In logic they state axiom and inference patterns, including modus ponens. In mathematics they can express theories with infinitely many axioms, such as first-order induction. The entry emphasizes that this differs from second-order induction: the first-order version generates many sentences, while the second-order version is a single sentence with a variable that ranges over properties or classes, and the two are not inferentially equivalent. In semantics, Tarski’s schema supplies a family of truth-related statements that an adequate definition of truth should entail. Philosophically, schemas have a mixed status: their templates are strings, while their conditions are more abstract. Their history reaches from ancient logical patterns to modern formal logic.
key_ideas: A schema is more than a template: its side conditions help determine the language and allowable substitutions.
Schemas must be distinguished from open sentences whose variables range over objects.
They can generate sentence, subsentence, and argument-text instances; modus ponens is a central example of the last kind.
In logic and mathematics, schemas can specify infinitely many axioms or inference rules.

A first-order induction schema is a recipe for producing sentences, whereas a second-order induction axiom is one sentence containing a genuine variable over properties or classes; the latter is logically stronger in the comparison described by the entry.
In semantics, Tarski’s pattern connects a sentence with its being true and serves as a requirement on an adequate truth definition.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schemas are a central tool for handling generality in formal reasoning. They make it possible to state a rule covering indefinitely many substitutions while exposing exactly how those substitutions work. They also force a useful distinction between language and metalanguage, between syntax and what expressions mean, and between a recipe for producing statements and a statement that quantifies over objects or properties.

important_terms.definition: A template together with conditions governing how its placeholders are filled to generate instances.
A completed sentence, formula, or argument produced from a schema under its side conditions.
A string of words or symbols containing marks that await permitted substitutions.
A condition specifying the language and the permitted substitutions, including restrictions on repeated placeholders.
A variable in the language being studied that ranges over objects in its domain.
A mark in a schema that stands for a syntactic expression to be inserted; it belongs to the metalanguage rather than the object language.
An argument pattern with premises above a line and a conclusion below it.
A sentence or argument pattern used to specify many axioms or inference cases at once.

questions_to_think_about: What information is supplied by a side condition that the template alone does not provide?
Why is a placeholder in a schema not the same as an object-language variable?
Why might a theory use an axiom schema instead of listing every axiom?
What changes when induction is expressed by a first-order schema rather than a second-order axiom?
Is a schema best understood as a pattern, its rules, or the set of instances it generates?

summaries.example: A school rule says: “If a student finishes A, then the student may begin B.” Suppose the rule requires the same activity to replace both uses of A. Replacing A with “the reading” and B with “the quiz” gives one instance. Replacing A with “the lab” gives another. The rule itself is not one of these classroom sentences; it is a pattern plus instructions about how to use it.
summaries.summary: A schema is a formal pattern that generates instances: particular sentences, expressions, or arguments. It contains a template with placeholders and a side condition explaining how those placeholders may be filled. For example, the pattern “Either A or not A” becomes a sentence only after the same suitable sentence is substituted for both occurrences of A. This is different from an open sentence such as an equation containing variables. Object-language variables range over objects, whereas schema placeholders stand for expressions. Schemas have several important uses. In logic, they state axiom patterns and inference rules. In mathematics, they can describe infinitely many axioms, as with first-order induction. In semantics, Tarski’s truth schema helps set a condition for an adequate definition of truth. The entry also distinguishes a first-order induction schema from a second-order induction axiom: one is a recipe producing sentences, while the other is a sentence involving a variable over properties or classes, and the second is stronger in the comparison given. Finally, the entry examines the ontology of schemas. A template is a string type with physical tokens, but its conditions are more abstract. Historical discussion connects modern schemas with earlier patterns in Aristotle’s logic and with developments in twentieth-century formal logic.
key_ideas: A schema combines a template with rules for filling it; the template alone may not determine the schema.
The same template can be associated with different schemata if the side conditions differ.
A schema is not automatically true or false, since it is not normally a complete assertion.
Object-language variables and schema placeholders may look alike but perform different jobs.
Schemas are useful in logic, mathematics, and theories of truth because they cover many cases efficiently.
Philosophers disagree about whether to identify a schema mainly with its template, its instances, or the whole template-and-condition system.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schemas provide a precise way to talk about general rules without pretending that a pattern is already a complete statement. They help formal systems manage infinitely many cases and clarify why substitution, variables, language, and meaning must not be confused. Their philosophical importance lies partly in this boundary between expressions in a language and the metalanguage used to describe how those expressions are formed.

important_terms.definition: A structured pattern with placeholders and rules that can produce many particular expressions.
A particular expression made by filling a schema’s placeholders correctly.
A blank, letter, or symbol used to mark where an expression may be inserted.
Instructions that control the language and substitutions allowed in a schema.
A sentence pattern that can generate many sentences when its placeholders are filled.
A pattern for premises and a conclusion, used to represent many arguments.
A pattern that specifies many axioms rather than being one axiom itself.
A formal language being discussed, as opposed to the language used to describe it.

questions_to_think_about: Why must repeated placeholders usually receive the same expression?
How could two different-looking templates generate the same collection of instances?
Why is an induction schema not simply the same as a single induction axiom?
What might be gained or lost by moving work from the object language to the metalanguage?
When is it more helpful to study the instances than the exact nature of the schema?
